These layers allow for the independent representation and manipulation of different types of contextual information -- temporal in the primary layer and semantic in the secondary layer. 
This separation has been justified on the grounds that it enables the model to capture the variability in clustering behavior seen across different types of memory tasks. 
For example, participants may exhibit variability in whether they cluster items based on their temporal proximity in a study list or their semantic relatedness, and CMR’s dual-layer structure accommodates this by allowing different forms of context to exert independent influences on recall [@morton2016predictive].
Participants may also exhibit variability in the extent to which context reinstated from earlier-than-most-recently recalled items influences the recall of subsequent items.
The dual-layer structure of CMR allows for the independent representation of context from different study events, enabling the model to capture differences in the persistence of temporal and semantic contextual influence in memory search.
The continuum hypothesis can be instantiated within this framework by representing repetition and similarity relationships between study events in the same secondary layer of context, but this approach leaves ambiguous just what kind of information is integrated by the primary layer of context.
Rather than item-specific information, the layer might more abstractedly represent the temporal relationships between items.
However, the focal claim in CMR's specification is that reinstated item-specific context itself -- rather than general temporal information -- is the primary source of temporal organization in memory search, suggesting a deeper tension than might be evident in the model's structure [@polyn2009context].

Given the importance of this distinction in previous work, it is critical to evaluate whether maintaining separate contextual layers is indeed necessary or whether alternative approaches could provide a more unified understanding of memory search. 
One such approach is to explore a single-layer model that modulates the similarity of contextual states based on item similarity. 
In this model, rather than separating temporal and semantic contexts into distinct layers, a unified context would dynamically adjust the degree of similarity or orthogonality between contextual states, depending on the features of the items being encoded.
This could be achieved by introducing a scaling factor that modulates the overlap in reinstated contextual features as a function of item similarity, thereby allowing the model to flexibly account for both repetition and similarity effects within a single framework.
If this and related approaches fail to capture the full range of effects observed in the data, it would provide strong evidence in favor of maintaining separate contextual layers in CMR and prompt reconceptualization of what the primary layer of context represents.

#### Alternative Approaches
A related but distinct approach to characterization of the relationship between temporal and semantic contiguity effects in memory search is to explore how retrieval cues interact during the recall process rather than how they are encoded during study
In an evaluation of competing specifications incorporating semantic organization in CMR, @morton2016predictive identified as the most successful model a variant where temporal and semantic cues act as separate but interacting sources of information that guide memory search. 
Their model suggests that while temporal contextual cues contact a context-to-item association memory to provide the organization of recall based on the sequence of study events, an additional cue based on the last recalled item contacts an item-to-item semantic association memory to help cluster items based on their relatedness or shared features.
The semantic memory contacted under this specification is inert during encoding, held out from contextual dynamics and associative processes that occur during study, and only becomes active during retrieval to support the organization of recall responses.
This variant of CMR conceptualized the simultaneous temporal and semantic organization of memory search as supported by a linear combination of these two sources of information, with the relative weighting of each cue parameterized by subject.

This approach is in tension with the continuum hypothesis about repetition and similarity effects because the retrieved context account of repetition effects typically centers on factors of contextual variability and reinstatement that are not applicable in a model that treats semantic organization as arising from a separate retrieval cue and memory structure.
Nonetheless, it is a viable alternative to the dual-layer specification of CMR that has been successful in previous work, and it is important to evaluate whether it can provide a more parsimonious account of the data.
Straightforward variants of the model can also alternatively accomodate the continuum hypothesis (e.g., by providing an account of repetition effects in terms of cues to semantic memory) or address tensions between repetition and semantic similarity effects in free recall. 
For example, rather than using a linear combination rule to integrate temporal and semantic cues, the model could use a multiplicative rule or switching mechanism [@hills2012optimal] to flexibly adjust the influence of each cue based on the features of the items being recalled.
Such an approach could account for the effect of massed presentation on semantic clustering by exaggerating the influence of semantic cues when items are presented in close temporal proximity, thereby promoting the recall of semantically related items.
The proposed experiment provides an opportunity to evaluate these and other alternative approaches to modeling memory search in the context of repetition and similarity effects, offering a comprehensive examination of how different assumptions about contextual dynamics influence the organization of recall responses.
